stories.headline: Republican senators criticize Trump's Russia sanctions waiver as Congress is in recess
stories.dek: Sens. Thom Tillis and Darline Graham were among the Republicans who criticized the waiver of a law the Senate passed 86-11, while the Senate holds only pro forma sessions until it returns on Nov. 9, after the Nov. 3 election.
whatsNew: On Oct. 16, President Trump issued an executive order waiving the duties and a long list of sanctions under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 (H.R. 5334, Public Law 119-111), a law he had signed on Sept. 18. [[c1]] Yesterday's edition covered the order itself; this story follows the reaction since then, much of it from Republican senators.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) wrote in a social media post on Oct. 17 (on X, according to Newsweek): "What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?" [[c4]] The figure refers to the Senate's passage of the bill on Aug. 7, roll call 224, which was 86-11. [[c3]]

Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) is the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, for whom the law is named; Reuters reports that she disagreed with Trump's decision. [[c8]] She told reporters on Oct. 17: "Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia," because "I don't trust Putin and I don't trust Russia," Reuters reported. [[c5]] According to Bloomberg, she also said that she and the President "share the same goal, which is to end the war and get gas and diesel prices down," and that whether to use the sanctions law is "up to him." [[c6]] She plans to speak with Trump about the decision during his visit next week. [[c7]] Bloomberg notes that she was appointed to fill her brother's seat and is running for a full term. [[c9]]

Other Republicans also commented. At least eight Republican senators, along with several House Republicans, have spoken out against the diesel deal or the waiver, according to Bloomberg. [[c12]] Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) wrote on X: "Lindsey would be appalled," Newsweek reported. [[c11]] Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) said on Fox News, "I think it was a mistake," adding that "the current path, unfortunately, just benefits Putin," according to Bloomberg. [[c10]] Rep. French Hill (R-Ark.) said he has requested a classified briefing on the rationale behind the decision, Bloomberg reported. [[c13]] Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said: "There's nothing America First about Trump caving to Putin and exempting Russia from US sanctions." [[c14]]

The administration is defending the move but leaving the outcome open. Trump told reporters on Oct. 17 that "it's a very good decision," according to Bloomberg. [[c15]] At his Mar-a-Lago club he also said, "A lot of you don't know what my decision is yet, but we'll figure it out," Reuters reported. [[c16]] Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the President will use up to 60 days to assess the economic impact of the waived sanctions and tariffs, according to Reuters. [[c17]] A White House spokeswoman said enforcing the sanctions now "would impede ongoing U.S. efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia" and that the President can use the authorities at any time, Newsweek reported. [[c18]] Rubio also defended the separate diesel deal: "That diesel is going to be sold one way or the other," according to Reuters. [[c42]]
whyItMatters: The 60-day figure is Rubio's description, not a term of the order. Section 4(d) sets no end date: the waivers "shall remain in effect until such time as the President or the Secretary of State, in consultation with the Secretary of the Treasury and the Trade Representative, as appropriate, determine that further action is appropriate." [[c19]] Reuters also noted that the order did not specify how long the waiver would last. [[c17]] The order hands the section 115 waiver authority to the Secretary of State, so Rubio, not only the President, can decide when it ends. [[c20]] The one Oct. 18 date in the order is the cutoff in section 2(b) for new purchases of Russian crude oil or natural gas that would trigger the duty on the largest importers, and that duty is among those the order waives. [[c21]]

The law's own provisions bear on what Congress can do. Section 115 of the law lets the President waive any sanction, restriction or duty once he sends Congress a written certification that the waiver is in the national interest and a report explaining it, and the order states that both were submitted. [[c22]] The law's review procedure applies only to terminations under section 117: a termination cannot take effect for 30 calendar days and can be blocked by a joint resolution of disapproval, while a section 115 waiver needs only the certification and report. [[c23]] The order also lists section 117 among the provisions it waives. [[c2]] The waivers came 28 days after Trump signed the law, using a power written into the law itself. [[c1]]

Senators had raised objections before the waiver. In a letter dated Oct. 13, three days before the order, senators of both parties told Trump that the deal he struck with Putin on Oct. 9 "will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans," and that Treasury's General License No. 135 "lifts sanctions on Russia's diesel exports." [[c24]] They asked him to "withdraw from this agreement, rescind General License No. 135, and execute the authorities provided under" the Graham Act. [[c25]] They wrote that Russian diesel "will offer limited to no relief to Americans" and called the deal "a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies." [[c26]] The letter reminded the President that both chambers passed the law "with resounding, bipartisan votes, clearly demonstrating our intent." [[c29]]

The letter's signature block, as published by Sen. Richard Blumenthal's office, names Democrats Richard Blumenthal, Jeanne Shaheen, Richard J. Durbin, Sheldon Whitehouse, Jack Reed and Christopher A. Coons and Republicans Thom Tillis, Susan M. Collins, Alan Armstrong, Lisa Murkowski and Mitch McConnell. [[c27]] NPR and Bloomberg describe it as a letter from 12 senators and also list Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) as a signer. [[c28]]

On the political context, Bloomberg writes that the decision threatens a new rift between the White House and its congressional allies, with Republicans at risk of losing their majorities on Nov. 3. [[c36]] Abroad, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote that the U.S. had decided "to completely ignore the Lindsey Graham law" just as Russia launched a massive strike on Ukraine's energy sector, according to Bloomberg. [[c37]] Kirill Dmitriev, an envoy of Vladimir Putin, called the suspension "an important and truly historic moment," Newsweek reported. [[c38]]
whatsNext: Congress is out of session. The Senate is holding only pro forma sessions with no business expected and returns for business on Nov. 9 at 3 p.m. [[c30]] The House meets on Oct. 19 in a pro forma session. [[c31]] Bloomberg concludes there is "little prospect of immediate action" to block the diesel deal. [[c32]]

Bills have been introduced. A group of House Democrats and one Republican, Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), introduced a bill on Oct. 16 to block Russian diesel imports, Bloomberg reported, adding that passage would be difficult and could require overcoming a veto. [[c33]] Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.) introduced H.R. 10828 on Oct. 15 to impose sanctions on Russian oil and gas extraction and refinement. [[c34]] Bacon also pointed to the power of the purse, writing that "many of us won't fund these things knowing he is propping up a dictator's invasion," according to Bloomberg. [[c35]]

Near-term markers are: Darline Graham's planned conversation with Trump during his visit next week [[c7]], and the review of up to 60 days that Rubio described, which could run past both the Nov. 3 election and the Senate's return on Nov. 9 if the full 60 days are used. [[c17]]
background: What the order waives: section 4 waives the duties in sections 112 and 113 and the sanctions in sections 102(a), 102(d), 102(e), 103 through 111 and 117 of the Act. [[c2]] It states that sanctions under earlier executive orders tied to the Russia national emergency, continued on March 24, 2026, are unaffected. [[c41]]

Votes on the law: the Senate passed H.R. 5334 86-11 on Aug. 7 [[c3]], and the House agreed to the Senate amendments 262-159 on Sept. 16. [[c39]] The law's sanctions division expires five years after enactment. [[c40]]

Waiver versus termination: a section 115 waiver suspends application of a measure after a certification and report; a section 117 termination ends it, but only after a 30-day review period during which Congress can enact a joint resolution of disapproval. [[c23]]

Congress wrote its own check on Russia sanctions relief into the Countering America's Adversaries Through Sanctions Act of 2017. Section 216, part of the Russia Sanctions Review Act of 2017, requires the President to report to Congress before terminating covered sanctions, waiving them with respect to a person, or taking certain licensing actions. [[h1]] A 30-day review period follows. [[h2]] During review the President may not act unless Congress enacts a joint resolution of approval. [[h3]] In a report to Congress dated Dec. 19, 2018, the President proposed terminating sanctions on En+ Group, UC Rusal and JSC EuroSibEnergo; on Jan. 4, 2019, Sen. Chuck Schumer introduced a resolution of disapproval (S.J.Res. 2). [[h4]] On Jan. 16, 2019, the Senate voted on cloture, which needed three-fifths. [[h5]] The vote was 57-42, short of the 60 needed, and the resolution did not advance. [[h6]]

Section 115 of the Graham Act lets the President waive any sanctions provision, restriction or duty, after he submits to Congress a written certification that the waiver is in the national interests and a report explaining its basis. [[p1]] CRS notes that through legislation Congress can shape sanctions objectives and set the conditions under which sanctions may be applied, waived, exempted, or terminated. [[p2]] Section 117 works differently: a termination takes effect only after a 30-day review, and an enacted joint resolution of disapproval can block it. [[p3]] A joint resolution of disapproval must name a termination of a specific section, so it does not reach a section 115 waiver. [[p4]]

stages.label: Duties and listed sanctions waived by executive order

relevance.reason: The only story today with a real congressional power question and broad independent coverage: Republican senators publicly opposing a waiver of a law they passed 86-11, with the EO text and the senators' letter as primary sources. Continuation of yesterday's lead with genuinely new reactions; the arbiter fetched the EO and confirmed it sets no 60-day limit.
relevance.dissent: Counter-agent: Rubio reportedly describes the waiver as a 60-day pause, so the framing (open-ended waiver vs. time-limited suspension) must be pinned to the executive order text. Resolved: the order (section 4(d)) sets no end date; the 60-day figure is attributed to Rubio via Reuters.
